title: SLO-driven inference messaging
content:
Context / problem statement:
Many engineering teams have moved from asking "what model should we use" to asking "can this model meet our application SLOs?" But the market messaging is still model-first and feature-first. That creates a gap: product teams need predictable latency, cost, and correctness guarantees for user-facing flows, not just better perplexity numbers.

One-line thesis (working):
From model outputs to product SLOs — Redwood turns variable model performance into predictable, measurable inference outcomes for engineering teams.

Top-level positioning pillars (for GTM copy and field scripts):
1) SLO Predictability: Redwood makes latency, availability, and quality SLOs first-class. Smart routing + multi-variant fallbacks keep apps within targets even when a model or zone degrades.
2) Cost Transparency & Controls: Unit economics are visible and actionable — batching, cache, and quantization suggestions translate directly to $/request guarantees.
3) Developer Ergonomics: Same API, same rollout semantics across hosted, dedicated, and private so engineers iterate quickly without ops hairballs.
4) Enterprise-Ready: Private network options, KMS integrations, and audit trails let security-conscious teams adopt without rebuilding infra.

Why this resonates (evidence + customer pain):
- Customers building chat, search, and agent surfaces measure their success in SLOs: median+tail latency, per-user cost budget, and quality regressions on core prompts.
- Competing vendors sell model access or GPU orchestration; they rarely connect those capabilities to application-level SLAs and predictable economics.
- Example anecdote (field): a SaaS seller reduced surprise bill spikes by 40% after adopting Redwood’s batching+cache recommendations and targeted routing for peak hours.

Key differentiators to call out (how to phrase):
- "Serving-as-a-contract": Redwood treats inference like a product-level contract (SLOs, rollouts, fallbacks), not just a compute endpoint.
- "Economics you can act on": Not raw perf numbers — actionable levers (batch size, cache TTL, quantization profile) and estimated dollar impact per change.
- "One interface, three modes": Self-serve hosted, reserved dedicated, and private deployment with identical API, dashboards, and rollout controls.

Competitive contrast (quick lines for field):
- vs. Managed cloud endpoints: They give VMs and models; Redwood gives application SLOs and automated fallback policies.
- vs. LLM API startups: They focus on model quality and tokens; Redwood focuses on keeping the product online and within cost targets.
- vs. Self-hosted runtimes: They offer kernels; Redwood offers runtime + orchestration + SLO automation so teams ship faster and operate with fewer surprises.

Leading with outcomes (sample headlines for different personas):
- Engineering lead: "Guarantee your app's latency and cost targets — even when models change."
- Platform/Infra: "Standardize inference across teams with predictable capacity and SLO-driven routing."
- Product manager: "Ship LLM features without surprise bills or tail latency regressions."

Proof points and evidence to surface in collateral: 
- Benchmarked tail latency under mixed workloads (internal chart placeholder).
- Case snippet: 40% fewer billing incidents; 25% lower p99 after enabling prefix cache on customer A.
- Product capability bullets mapping to SLOs: routing/fallbacks -> availability SLOs; batching/caching -> cost SLOs; rollout controls -> quality SLOs.

Objections and suggested responses (field-ready):
- "We can just control this ourselves with k8s + autoscale": Sure — but that leaves you rebuilding observability, rollback semantics, and SLO-aware routing. Redwood packages those patterns and integrates them into dev workflow.
- "We care about model choice, not serving": Model choice matters, but variability in serving (latency, cache warmups, failed nodes) is what breaks UX. We remove that operational surprise.
- "Hosted APIs are risky for compliance": We offer Dedicated and Private with identical API and control plane so you can keep data on-prem/VPC while still getting the runtime benefits.

Sample short pitches (A/B test candidates):
- A (SLO-first): "Stop guessing if your LLM will meet users' expectations — guarantee it with SLO-driven inference"
- B (Economics-first): "Lower per-user inference costs without raising latency — automated batching, caching, and routing."
- C (Ops-first): "Replace firefights with policies: canary rollouts, automatic fallbacks, and transparent cost impact."

Content/asset ideas to validate this messaging in Q1:
- One-pager: "SLO playbook for inference" (audience: engineering leads) — step-by-step mapping from SLO to config change.
- Short video: demo of an automated fallback saving an app during a cold-started model.
- Interactive calc: input traffic profile -> output estimated $/user with suggested optimizations.

Activation script for AE/SEs (checklist):
- Ask: what SLOs (latency, cost per user, inference quality) do you measure today?
- Show: a dashboard with per-route SLOs and a recent rollback/canary example.
- Validate: propose a 30-day pilot focusing on one user journey with targets for p50/p95/p99 and cost cap.

Measurement & success metrics for GTM experiments:
- Landing page conversion: +CTRs for SLO-first headline vs model-first control.
- AE win-rate lift in deals referencing "predictability" in discovery.
- Number of pilots that request Dedicated or Private after seeing SLO dashboards.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need a compact benchmarking artifact that translates dev-facing metrics (p99 tokens, amortized GPU utilization) into a customer-facing SLO chart. Who on eng can produce a 1-pager? (cc: @Diego)
- Decide whether "SLO" is too jargony for some buyer segments — keep a variant that uses "reliability & cost guarantees". Run ad copy tests.
- Create a short field kit (1 slide + 1 demo script + 2 customer rebuttals).

Notes to self (informal):
- Avoid leading with "models" — lead with product outcomes.
- Use concrete dollar or latency numbers where available in case studies; abstract claims feel hollow.

Next steps (owners):
- Draft the one-pager + interactive calc: Priya -> by 2025-02-14.
- Benchmark artifact: Eng liaison (Leo) -> by 2025-02-28.
- Field kit and A/B copy tests: Diego + AE bench -> kickoff 2025-02-10.

End of brief.
